AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Amazon ↗ Open Full Page

Optimize AI economics on Amazon Bedrock with Accenture’s sequenced approach

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1988 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Amazon

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • As enterprises scale AI on Amazon Bedrock, token spend often grows even as per-token prices fall.
  • In this post, you will learn about six levers for optimizing token spend, how Accenture applied them in production, and how to apply them using Amazon Bedrock.
  • Accenture applied these levers in four client engagements across telecom, insurance, mining, and a large enterprise deployment.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

As enterprises scale AI on Amazon Bedrock, token spend often grows even as per-token prices fall. Without cost allocation tags in place, your cloud invoice demonstrates AI spend as a single line item rather than by team, workload, agent, or model. Cheaper tokens expand adoption, and agentic workloads multiply invocations. As successful AI use cases scale, consumption can rise faster than unit prices drop. The economic question is whether the business value generated grows faster than the cost of the intelligence required to produce it. The Linux Foundation has launched the Tokenomics Foundation to develop open standards for AI cost economics, a sign that managing the economics of AI is now an industry discipline.

In this post, you will learn about six levers for optimizing token spend, how Accenture applied them in production, and how to apply them using Amazon Bedrock.

Accenture applied these levers in four client engagements across telecom, insurance, mining, and a large enterprise deployment. The same levers are available natively on Amazon Bedrock as described in this post. Where savings were measured, token spend fell by about 40–85 percent. Results are specific to each client’s workload and may vary. Client names are withheld by Accenture to protect client confidentiality.

Sources indicate that before you optimize anything, you need to see where consumption is occurring, who owns it, and what business value it produces. Cost allocation tags at the team, workload, and agent level are the prerequisite for connecting consumption to accountable owners and, ultimately, to business outcomes. You apply them through Amazon Bedrock application inference profiles, one profile per application or workload, tagged by team, cost center, and environment. After you activate them as cost allocation tags in the AWS Billing and Cost Management console, you can use these tags to trace which teams, applications, and agents are driving spend. They also make it possible to measure the impact of each change you introduce.

Three AWS services provide the underlying telemetry. AWS Cost and Usage Reports (CUR 2.0), delivered through AWS Data Exports, handle financial attribution, breaking down billed inference cost by workload and team after your cost allocation tags are active. Amazon CloudWatch captures operational signals such as invocation counts and latency. Amazon Bedrock model invocation logging records request-level detail, including the model used and the input and output token counts for each call.

It has been revealed that telemetry alone isn’t enough. Engineers can read cost per invocation on a dashboard, but product owners and program leaders need a metric expressed in business terms. Accenture’s Cost per Business Transaction (CpBT) framework bridges this gap. CpBT aggregates all the model invocations, retries, tool calls, and agent handoffs that contribute to one successful business output into a single fully loaded cost figure. It surfaces the true cost of producing a result, including the failed attempts that raw token pricing hides. Tracked against the business value each workflow delivers, CpBT distinguishes a growing bill that reflects scaling success from one that reflects waste.

The goal of these six levers isn’t to minimize tokens at all costs. It’s to use the right amount and level of intelligence to deliver each business outcome at the appropriate cost, quality, and risk. The levers are organized into three phases based on the complexity of the change and the investment it requires. AWS and Accenture recommend working through the phases in order, and you can apply each phase independently to the workloads where it will have the most impact.

It has been revealed that with Amazon Bedrock prompt caching, the model reuses the parts of a prompt that repeat across requests, such as system instructions, tool definitions, and reference documents, so you stop paying full price to process the same content again. Amazon Bedrock stores the key-value state of previously computed prompt prefixes and is designed to skip recomputation on later requests. This is designed to reduce cached input token costs by up to 90 percent for supported models (see Amazon Bedrock Prompt Caching).

Amazon Bedrock batch inference processes non-urgent workloads asynchronously as a group at 50 percent lower cost than on-demand pricing for select models (see Amazon Bedrock Pricing). You submit inference requests as a batch job, and results are written to Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) when processing completes. Batch inference suits nightly reports, document processing pipelines, and evaluation runs that don’t need an immediate response.

It has been revealed that both levers add configuration to your existing setup. Prompt caching requires cache checkpoint markers in your prompts, and batch inference requires submitting eligible requests as a batch job instead of calling the on-demand API. Apply caching to interactive, on-demand traffic and batch inference to asynchronous work. Neither requires latest infrastructure or architecture changes.

Recent findings suggest that amazon Bedrock intelligent prompt routing directs requests across models within the same family, matching each task to the level of intelligence its business value, complexity, and risk require, rather than defaulting every request to the most powerful model. Intelligent prompt routing can reduce costs by up to 30 percent without compromising accuracy (see Amazon Bedrock intelligent prompt routing). Check Amazon Bedrock Pricing for any routing charges. In the following engagements, Accenture’s model tiering and triage routing apply this same routing lever.

Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) optimization tunes the retrieval step in the RAG process so that fewer unnecessary context tokens reach the model. Techniques such as hierarchical chunking, metadata-based filtering, and reranking narrow the retrieved context to the most relevant chunks, so you pay primarily for content that improves the answer.

It has been revealed that two complementary Accenture patterns work alongside these AWS native levers. Context scoping limits the data each agent receives to the document slice relevant to its step of the workflow, rather than passing the full case context at every handoff. Context compression summarizes or filters documents before they reach the model. Both reduce input token volume, especially across multi-agent chains.

Sources indicate that semantic caching stores responses and reuses them when a new request is semantically similar to one already answered, even if the wording differs. This avoids redundant model invocations and reduces both cost and latency. On AWS, you can implement it with a vector store such as Amazon ElastiCache in front of the model. In an AWS benchmark on 63,796 real chatbot queries, a 0.90 similarity threshold produced a 74.5 percent cache hit rate, 92.3 percent accuracy, and 72.5 percent cost savings (see ElastiCache semantic caching benchmarks). As you apply routing and semantic caching, keep Amazon Bedrock Guardrails on every route, and set semantic cache expiry so that owners don’t receive outdated answers.

Model distillation transfers knowledge from a large teacher model to a smaller, faster student model. Distilled models in Amazon Bedrock are up to 500 percent faster and up to 75 percent less expensive than original models, with less than 2 percent accuracy loss for use cases such as RAG. Distillation is best suited to stable, high-volume workloads where the transaction volume justifies the training investment.

Sources indicate that accenture applied these levers in four client engagements. Each engagement targeted a different cost pattern. In two of them, Accenture applied several changes together, so those results reflect the combined effect rather than any single lever.

It has been revealed that the first engagement was a large enterprise deployment where every request went to a frontier model, with no caching, model tiering, or batching. Accenture applied three changes together: model tiering to match each task to the smallest model that could handle it well, prompt caching for repeated context, and batch processing for overnight and non-urgent jobs. Together they cut monthly token cost by 85 percent, and the saving was not separated by change. About 15 percent of tasks still needed the top model for hard, open-ended reasoning, and the rest ran on lighter models. Your split will depend on your workload composition.

According to recent reports, the second engagement was a telecom operator with $12 million in annual token spend. Most of that spend came from agents fanning out requests without limits and from every request going to a frontier model regardless of complexity. Accenture applied triage routing, semantic caching, and context compression together. Input tokens fell by 70 percent, and annual token spend fell from $12 million to $3.8 million, a 68 percent reduction. Accenture validated output quality against the operator’s pre-change performance benchmarks.

In a recent development, the third and fourth engagements each applied a single cache layer. An insurer used model-layer prefix caching, reusing the static portions of its prompts across invocations. A mining operator used an application-layer semantic cache, returning stored responses for repeated queries before they reached the model. Across the two engagements, token spend fell by about 40 percent combined, without model routing changes or training investment.

In a recent development, outcomes ranged from about 40 percent to about 85 percent, reflecting each client’s starting point. The large enterprise deployment began with no optimization in place and reached 85 percent. The telecom operator reached 68 percent on $12 million in annual token spend, and the insurer and mining operator reached about 40 percent combined with one caching lever each. Results are specific to each client’s workload and may vary.

According to recent reports, these savings aren’t the end goal. They create capacity to scale AI workloads, reinvest in higher-value use cases, and improve the return generated by each dollar of AI consumption. Two of these engagements applied several changes at once. When you apply one lever at a time, you can attribute each result to a specific change. AWS and Accenture recommend this sequence for your own workloads: connect consumption to owners and outcomes, apply one lever at a time, measure cost, quality, and business value, and build on what works.

According to recent reports, optimizing AI economics in production requires an ongoing governance cycle spanning cost, quality, risk, and business value, not a one-time technical change. Before you apply any lever, establish a quantitative baseline for both cost and quality so that you can measure the impact of each change against a known starting point. When you validate output quality, use held-out evaluation sets drawn from your actual production traffic rather than synthetic benchmarks. Apply one lever at a time per workload so that you can attribute results to a specific change and roll back cleanly if quality drops below your acceptable thresholds. If you operate in a regulated industry such as financial services, insurance, or healthcare, document your quality test results and rollback procedures as part of your standard change management record.

These four tenets apply regardless of which levers you are using or what phase of the sequencing you are in. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore is an environment where you can build, connect, and optimize agents at scale with any framework or model. It includes AgentCore Evaluations, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore that provides batch evaluation to support your quality validation cycle as you progress through more advanced levers.

Recent findings suggest that you can begin with three steps. First, turn on cost attribution for Amazon Bedrock by applying cost allocation tags at the team and workload level so that your spend is traceable from day one. Second, activate those tags in the AWS Billing and Cost Management console. Then use CUR 2.0 and model invocation logging to identify high-consumption workloads, and assess each one based on spend, business value, quality requirements, risk, volume, and optimization potential. Third, apply Amazon Bedrock prompt caching to that workload’s interactive traffic and Amazon Bedrock batch inference to its asynchronous jobs as configuration-only changes, and measure the result before you move to architectural changes in Phase 2.

The AWS Well-Architected Agentic AI Lens includes model invocation and token cost optimization (AGENTCOST02), a focus area within the cost optimization pillar for agentic workloads. This focus area provides a structured framework you can use to apply these levers at scale across your organization.

Welcome Le Chonk: Mistral Large 4 on Hugging Face

📅 29 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1582 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Mistral Large 4 (aka Le Chonk) is a multimodal, multilingual, Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model from Mistral.
  • There are also GGUFs created by Unsloth and the llama.cpp team.
  • Mistral Large 4 is particularly strong for cybersecurity, coding agents, and multimodality.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Mistral Large 4 (aka Le Chonk) is a multimodal, multilingual, Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model from Mistral. It takes text and images as input and generates text. It has about 1T total, 49B active parameter, and a context window of 1M tokens.

The model is released in two official variants:.

There are also GGUFs created by Unsloth and the llama.cpp team. It’s distributed under the Mistral Ecosystem Open-Weight License (an MIT derivative that establishes limitations for model-as-a-service offerings).

Mistral Large 4 is particularly strong for cybersecurity, coding agents, and multimodality. In this post, we look at how the model works, its capabilities, architecture and more!

Sources indicate that mistral Large 4 combines a large pool of experts with sparse attention and a Pixtral vision encoder. The language model selects a small group of experts for each token, while its attention indexer selects which earlier token positions to attend to. These are two different forms of sparsity, where one selects feed-forward networks, the other selects context positions.

You can find all the checkpoints in the Mistral Large 4 collection.

According to recent reports, mistral Large 4 scores 82% on the Artificial Analysis Cyber Index test that asks a model to reproduce a real vulnerability in open-source software and then patch the software. Mistral reports that several closed frontier models score near zero on the same test because they refuse to attempt the work. This is super important for defenders, because fixing a vulnerability usually requires reproducing the vulnerability. In Mistral’s internal testing, Mistral Large 4 was also useful for malware analysis, vulnerability prioritisation and writing detection rules, which the model was not explicitly trained for.

Mistral mainly positions the model for defensive security work. Vulnerability research and incident response often appear like attacks in model input, so closed source filters can block them. A team that depends on an API can also lose access in the middle of an incident. Crucially, open weight models put both the usage policy and the deployment under the user’s control. That remarked, the model still declines harmful requests: on cyber prompts from JailbreakBench, StrongREJECT and AgentHarm, its average refusal rate is higher than any other open weight model.

For community builders, an open weight model like Mistral Large 4 unlocks a load of downstream use cases. You could build your own cyber system around your code base, crash logs, and malware samples. For example, with TRL you could fine-tune smaller models from Mistral Large 4 traces patching your code base. In fact, reproduce-then-patch tasks use a verifiable reward, so it fits with RL environments that could be used to further RL smaller security models. Open weights also let researchers measure the model’s refusal behaviour directly instead of relying on the provider’s description.

In short, cyber capabilities like ML4’s in the open are a huge boost for the community.

We have interviewed Pierre Stock about the cyber capabilities of the model, you can watch it here.

It has been revealed that mistral Large 4’s text decoder has 72 layers, a hidden dimension of 6,144, and 64 attention heads. Its attention blocks combine Multi-head Latent Attention (MLA) with a DeepSeek Sparse Attention (DSA) indexer (a direction in other models such as GLM 5.3). MLA keeps a compressed KV representation, and DSA selects up to 2,048 key positions for each query.

According to recent reports, for each decoder block, there’s a 3:1 RoPE to NoPE pattern, i.e. 3 decoder layers employ RoPE and every fourth layer uses NoPE. The model also shares KV state across layers.The first decoder layer uses a dense feed-forward network. The other 71 layers use MoE blocks, in which a softmax router selects four of the 128 experts for each token. One shared expert always runs alongside the selected experts, for a total of 5 active experts per token.

Regarding RoPE, Mistral uses LeRope, a YaRN-scaled RoPE with one learned multiplier per frequency.

It has been revealed that mistral Large 4 employs a 1.6B Pixtral encoder. Pixtral has 30 layers, a hidden dimension of 2,048, and 16 attention heads. It uses 14 × 14 patches and a patch-merge projector with spatial merge size 2. You can see the encoder pipeline below.

Mistral Large 4 delivers strong benchmark performance across coding, cybersecurity, multimodal understanding, and agentic workflows, positioning it as a competitive addition to the open-weight ecosystem. As of October 29, 2026, the model is the fifth best open weights model on Artificial Analysis Intelligence index.

On coding, ML4 achieves 61.7% on DeepSWE v1.1, 59.4% on SWE-Atlas-QnA, and 28.3% on Terminal-Bench 4. Its combined Coding Agent Index score of 49.8% places it ahead of DeepSeek V4 Pro 0813 and Qwen3.8 Max.

Coding capabilities of ML4 extend to knowledge work, with 59.9% on AutomationBench and 1,393 Elo on AA-Briefcase, which evaluate business workflows and long-horizon professional tasks.

Recent findings suggest that cybersecurity is one of Mistral Large 4’s standout capabilities, with strong results across real-world vulnerability assessment and security competition tasks. Three benchmarks highlight the model’s cyber performance:.

In a recent development, mistral Large 4 also demonstrates 93.3% attack resistance on Lakera’s B3 benchmark, adding evidence of robustness against prompt-injection attacks. Beyond benchmarks, internal testing demonstrated promising results in malware analysis, vulnerability prioritization, and detection-rule generation.

Mistral Large 4 is shipped with day-0 support for transformers, vLLM and llama.cpp. GGUF quants are available from GGUF and the llama.cpp team. We provide options to deploy remotely with Inference Endpoints, and use serverless inference through Inference Providers.

The Transformers implementation provides AutoModelForMultimodalLM, with AutoProcessor preparing the conversation and image inputs. Mistral Large 4 can take low, medium, high as reasoning effort. The default is high, and note that reasoning cannot be disabled, so using reasoning_effort: none would still use high.

Latest Update: Amazon Polly introduces voice cloning: A unique voice for your brand

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1390 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Amazon

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that voice cloning in Amazon Polly is now generally available as a gated release.
  • In a recent development, amazon Polly voice cloning is available in all the AWS Regions supported by the Amazon Polly generative engine, including the AWS GovCloud (US) Region.
  • Industry observers note that with this upcoming feature addition, you can build the cloning lifecycle into AWS applications.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that voice cloning in Amazon Polly is now generally available as a gated release. Give Amazon Polly a few minutes of audio recordings from a speaker who has agreed to have their voice cloned, and Amazon Polly builds your own cloned voice in that speaker’s voice. The cloned voices run on the Amazon Polly generative engine, which delivers similar naturalness and accuracy as the rest of the generative voices. Amazon Polly voice cloning launches with seven languages: English, Spanish, German, French, Italian, Portuguese, and Hindi. Each cloned voice speaks the language it was recorded in. The cloned voices are automatically encrypted and access-controlled: only you can access your cloned voices.

In a recent development, amazon Polly voice cloning is available in all the AWS Regions supported by the Amazon Polly generative engine, including the AWS GovCloud (US) Region. Access is already enabled for select Amazon Polly customers. Others can reach out to their AWS account team or apply for access to get access.

Industry observers note that with this upcoming feature addition, you can build the cloning lifecycle into AWS applications. Building a cloned voice is free for Amazon Polly customers, and Amazon Polly charges for cloned voice usage on a pay-as-you-go basis, see Amazon Polly Pricing page for details.

Press play: the first few seconds are a real recording of the speaker, and then their cloned voice takes over with words they never recorded.

A consistent brand voice across channels.

Establish one recognizable voice and use it across your interactive voice response (IVR) system, cascaded voice agents, mobile app, in-store announcements, advertising, and connected devices. Rather than relying on a generic stock voice or re-booking a recording session each time a script changes, you can generate on-brand audio on demand, with a consistent sound in every channel.

Deliver a distinctive, on-brand voice across self-service flows, and update prompts as offers and policies change without a latest studio session. You can create prompts from source text, test them before rollout, and use the same voice across greeting, routing, and notification experiences.

Creators, publishers, and studios can create audiobooks, courses, podcasts, game characters, and videos in multiple custom voices to enhance the listening experience, and produce subsequent chapters or updates rapidly.

Localization with a consistent persona.

In a recent development, maintain a recognizable voice identity across a content library, so narration remains coherent across titles and updates. Each cloned voice speaks only the language it was recorded in. For multilingual experiences, create and review approved voices per supported language.

Accessibility and personalization.

Offer a natural, human-sounding voice for reading experiences, assistive tools, and personalized interactions. You confirm the speaker’s consent each time you create a voice.

Recent findings suggest that with voice cloning, you can build a custom Amazon Polly voice from recordings of a single speaker and then synthesize speech in that voice through the Amazon Polly generative engine. The voice moves through four steps, from recording the speaker to using the finished voice:.

Figure 1: The voice cloning lifecycle, from recording a speaker to using the finished voice.

A cloned voice goes through four steps:.

Sources indicate that A cloned voice is made from one person’s recordings. You confirm that you have the speaker’s consent for all recordings and that you control who can use the voice and when it’s deleted.

For details on intended uses and limitations, see the Amazon Polly AI Service Card and the AWS Responsible Use of AI guidance.

Your cloned voice learns from the recording, including the parts you’d rather it didn’t: the laptop fan, the room echo, the meeting app’s noise filter.

Industry observers note that on the console: once voice cloning is enabled for your account (see Availability), expand the left panel and choose Voice cloning, upload up to 10 recordings or select them from Amazon S3, confirm the terms, and choose Create. Each upload can be up to 5 MB. When the voice is ready, try it out on its details page.

If Python reports that the Polly object has no attribute create_voice, upgrade boto3.

For long texts such as audiobook chapters or course modules, use an asynchronous synthesis task that writes the audio to S3:.

For additional end-to-end Speech AI applications you can build with Amazon Polly, including the voice cloning feature, such as cascaded voice agents and live speech translators, go to the Amazon Polly GitHub repo.

Voice creation takes minutes, so treat it as a provisioning step, not part of a user request. A small workflow (for example, AWS Step Functions or a job queue) can call CreateVoice, check GetVoice every 30 seconds until the voice is active, and then store the voice ID in your configuration. CreateVoice and DeleteVoice share a limit of 1 request per second, so queue bulk creations and deletions.

Sources indicate that describeVoices lists your cloned voices alongside the voices built into Amazon Polly. Cloned voices have Origin set to customer. Store the voice ID, Region, language, consent reference, and owner for each voice, and give each voice a unique Name. If a CreateVoice call times out or returns a server error, the voice might already exist, and the SDK’s automatic retries can create a second one. Check DescribeVoices for that name before you try again.

CreateVoice returns ThrottlingException when you exceed the 1-request-per-second limit it shares with DeleteVoice, and ServiceQuotaExceededException when the account has reached its cloned-voice quota in that Region. Synthesizing with, or deleting, a voice that is still being created returns ConflictException. If a voice uses your own KMS key, callers without access to the key get an access-denied error. When creation fails, StatusReason gives only a general message, so check the recordings against the preceding recording best practices, then delete the failed voice and create a newly introduced one.

Cloned voices are IAM resources, so you can give the role that serves traffic permission to synthesize with one voice of choice. If the voice uses your own KMS key, that role also needs access to the key. Keep polly:CreateVoice and polly:DeleteVoice for a separate provisioning role. Here’s an example policy for the serving role:.

In a recent development, with tags, you can write the same rule once for a whole group of voices using aws:ResourceTag conditions. Review your existing policies too: a statement that allows polly:SynthesizeSpeech on all resources ("Resource": "*") also covers every cloned voice in the account.

Each account has an initial quota of 10 cloned voices per Region. To request an increase, contact your account team or AWS Support. A voice exists only in the account and Region where you created it. To serve another Region or account, create the voice again in that Region from the same recordings, and make sure the speaker’s consent covers every copy.

Before a voice goes live, listen to it reading your own content: product names, numbers, addresses, and the longest sentences you have. The same text can come out slightly differently from one request to the next. For fixed prompts such as phone-line greetings, generate the audio once, approve it with the speaker and your brand team, and serve the stored file. If a name or term comes out wrong, spell it differently in the text or use a Speech Synthesis Markup Language (SSML) tag. Phoneme tags work with cloned voices in English, French, Italian, German, and Spanish. See Supported SSML tags.

Voice cloning in Amazon Polly gives your application a voice people recognize: recorded once, with the speaker’s consent, and ready to use through the Amazon Polly APIs. To get started on the console, make sure Voice cloning is enabled for your account, prepare a recording and the required consent, open the Amazon Polly console, and create your first cloned voice. If you are a upcoming customer and would like to enable voice cloning, reach out to your AWS account team or apply for access to get access.

It has been revealed that for the developer guide, refer to the Amazon Polly documentation. For pricing, see the Amazon Polly Pricing Page. For additional speech AI use cases you can build with Amazon Polly, including voice cloning, check out the GitHub repo.

We can’t wait to hear what you build.

Thanks to Trevor Wood, Jonas Rohnke, Suyin Wang, Hannah Barrett, Nikie Xiong, Jeff Barr, and Joely Huang for lending us their voices.

#8727. Announcing Project ProtoStar: Making Publicly Funded Science AI-Ready

📅 29 Oct 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1303 w)

AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

Announcing Project ProtoStar: Making Publicly Funded Science AI-Ready

📅 29 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1303 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • An initiative bringing together universities, research organizations, industry, and the open science community to make publicly funded research easier to discover, reuse, and build upon.
  • According to recent reports, today, we're announcing Project ProtoStar, an initiative to unlock the potential of publicly funded scientific research by making datasets, models, and code more accessible and reusable, particularly for AI-driven research.
  • The initiative's founding partners include Carnegie Mellon University, Purdue University, Georgia Institute of Technology, Arizona State University, and The George Washington University, all working through the Open Forum for AI (OFAI) as the university coalition partner; the Astera Institute; Hugging Face as the infrastructure partner; and the Open Research Community Accelerator (ORCA), through its Fostering Innovation Network, as the community partner.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

An initiative bringing together universities, research organizations, industry, and the open science community to make publicly funded research easier to discover, reuse, and build upon.

According to recent reports, today, we're announcing Project ProtoStar, an initiative to unlock the potential of publicly funded scientific research by making datasets, models, and code more accessible and reusable, particularly for AI-driven research. ProtoStar brings together research institutions, industry, and the open science community to support the release of scientific artifacts in AI-ready, machine-actionable formats, and to demonstrate their value through a series of open challenges. The first challenge, hosted by Carnegie Mellon University, opens on November 2. See How to Participate below.

The initiative's founding partners include Carnegie Mellon University, Purdue University, Georgia Institute of Technology, Arizona State University, and The George Washington University, all working through the Open Forum for AI (OFAI) as the university coalition partner; the Astera Institute; Hugging Face as the infrastructure partner; and the Open Research Community Accelerator (ORCA), through its Fostering Innovation Network, as the community partner.

Recent findings suggest that participating organizations formalize their involvement through a memorandum of understanding supporting the release of suitable scientific datasets, models, and code in AI-ready formats on open infrastructure. Organizations interested in joining Project ProtoStar can reach out to protostar@orcaopen.org.

The U.S. federal government invests approximately $190 billion annually in research and development, and federal policy increasingly expects the results to be shared publicly. Agencies such as the National Institutes of Health (NIH) and National Science Foundation (NSF) have strengthened public-access requirements for funded research publications and require researchers to blueprint for sharing the underlying data. Hugging Face is among the ten generalist repositories listed by NIH for sharing research data.

It has been revealed that but making research publicly available does not automatically make it usable. Scientific datasets, models, and code are often scattered across incompatible systems, stored in static or legacy formats, or released without the documentation, metadata, and provenance needed to understand and reuse them. These limitations make it harder for researchers to build on existing work, and harder still for AI systems to discover, interpret, and combine scientific resources across disciplines.

Industry observers note that project ProtoStar aims to help close this gap by encouraging systematic sharing of publicly funded scientific artifacts in AI-ready formats, supported by open infrastructure and practical publishing guidance. It builds on efforts such as the National Cancer Institute's AI Data-Readiness Challenge and Hugging Face's guide to preparing public-sector data for AI. The goal is to make it easier for research organizations to meet existing public-access expectations while increasing the scientific value of the work they release.

The demand for reusable scientific resources is already evident. Hugging Face hosts more than 17,000 public datasets across core scientific domains, including genomics, protein design, chemistry, weather and climate, Earth observation, and astronomy. That figure approaches 29,000 when medicine and mathematics are included, alongside a comparable number of scientific models.

According to recent reports, the pace of sharing is also accelerating. Researchers shared more than three times as many newly introduced science datasets on Hugging Face in the first nine months of 2026 as in the same period of 2025, with growth remaining substantial even after excluding the largest individual uploader.

Figure 1. New public science datasets on Hugging Face per quarter, by domain (Q1 2023–Q3 2026). Counts datasets still public, by creation date. Source: Hugging Face Hub data, October 2026. Explore the data.

When organizations share research in reusable formats, the scientific community can build on it at scale. The 18 public repositories maintained by NIH's National Center for Biotechnology Information (NCBI) on Hugging Face have collectively received more than 11 million downloads, while NASA IMPACT's 27 repositories have received approximately 770,000 downloads, as of October 26, 2026. Documentation is also an important part of making these resources useful: 90% of dataset downloads on Hugging Face are from fully documented datasets.

In a recent development, publicly available genomic data has proved key in contributing to research that further advances fields such as biological research; researchers at Hugging Face have been building on openly available scientific resources, including recent releases from HuggingFaceBio such as Carbon-A and Carbon-X. By releasing the resulting models, datasets, and tools openly, these efforts demonstrate how existing scientific resources can support newly introduced research that others can build upon.

This is the kind of activity that we are further catalyzing via Project ProtoStar through institutional policies adopted by participating orgs. As an early example of institutional commitment, CMU's Open Source Programs Office is encouraging its researchers to share suitable datasets, AI models, and other research outputs on Hugging Face, while recognizing the continued importance of domain-specific repositories.

Making scientific artifacts AI-ready is an crucial first step. We also want to demonstrate what researchers, developers, and the broader scientific community can accomplish when those resources are made available for reuse.

A central question for ProtoStar is: Can publicly funded scientific datasets, models, and code, released in AI-ready formats, be readily discovered, reused, combined, and extended to accelerate scientific discovery and public benefit?

Recent findings suggest that to explore this, ProtoStar will organize a series of open challenges, each hosted by a participating research institution and built around scientific resources that the institution has released openly. The challenges have two complementary goals:.

The resulting projects and lessons learned will help build a practical evidence base for making publicly funded science more accessible and useful.

Hosted by Carnegie Mellon University | November 2–13, 2026.

Sources indicate that the inaugural ProtoStar challenge invites participants to test whether AI can improve predictions of urban climate conditions using historical weather data from 210 U.S. cities. Building on research by Carnegie Mellon University, teams will use climate records through 2018 to predict actual conditions from 2019 to 2026, allowing their models to be evaluated against observed weather rather than hypothetical future scenarios.

In a recent development, participants will forecast four indicators relevant to urban planning: average annual temperature, total annual precipitation, the hottest day of the year, and cooling degree days, a measure of demand for air conditioning. Their predictions will be compared against simple statistical baselines, including historical averages and linear trends, to assess whether AI approaches offer meaningful improvements in accuracy.

Beyond forecasting, participants will also propose a short climate adaptation policy idea informed by what they learned from the data. This component encourages teams to connect scientific analysis with practical public benefits, such as preparing cities for extreme heat, improving energy efficiency, or managing changing precipitation patterns.

Teams will submit a Hugging Face dataset with these outputs. Forecasting performance will be assessed through a public leaderboard measuring prediction errors against established baselines, while policy ideas will receive separate consideration. Final forecasting results will be published in early 2027, once the complete 2026 weather records are available.

Explore the CMU Climate Risk Intelligence Challenge.

Recent findings suggest that the CMU challenge is the first in this series. Other participating institutions will host their own challenges sequentially, each highlighting different publicly funded scientific resources and opportunities for reuse. Future challenges will be confirmed through the Project ProtoStar page on Hugging Face.

Whether you're an academic researcher, student, independent developer, or company building on open scientific infrastructure, ProtoStar offers opportunities to put publicly funded research to work and help us learn what is needed to make AI-ready open science more widely useful.

We also welcome universities, federal research agencies, national laboratories, nonprofits, and other research organizations interested in making their scientific resources more accessible and reusable. To explore participation or collaboration, reach out to protostar@orcaopen.org.

Our hope is that ProtoStar will make it easier for publicly funded scientific work to reach the people and tools that can build on it, while generating practical evidence about the infrastructure and practices needed to support open science at scale.

Tech Report: Amazon Bedrock AgentCore harness adds Strands harness defaults, built-in tools, and lifecycle hooks

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1370 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Amazon

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • When building an AI agent, selecting a model is only the first step.
  • Recent findings suggest that we are upgrading Amazon Bedrock AgentCore harness to use Strands harness, our open-source agent harness, released earlier this year, available under an Apache 2.0 license.
  • It has been revealed that with this upgrade, agents that rely on the managed defaults get a recommended model, a task-oriented system prompt, automatic prompt caching (initially for Anthropic models on Amazon Bedrock), and proactive context management.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

When building an AI agent, selecting a model is only the first step. The agent still needs tools, instructions for finishing the job, a way to manage context growth in long sessions, and guardrails before it executes any consequential actions, like issuing a refund.

Recent findings suggest that we are upgrading Amazon Bedrock AgentCore harness to use Strands harness, our open-source agent harness, released earlier this year, available under an Apache 2.0 license. AgentCore harness also introduces lifecycle hooks, so you can apply your own deterministic checks and notifications at defined points in the agent loop.

It has been revealed that with this upgrade, agents that rely on the managed defaults get a recommended model, a task-oriented system prompt, automatic prompt caching (initially for Anthropic models on Amazon Bedrock), and proactive context management. They also get additional built-in tools for planning, web retrieval, filesystem access, context offloading, and task delegation. This gives agents greater capabilities during long tasks, allowing them to keep track of subtasks, reduce context window usage, and delegate work. With hooks, you can transform non-deterministic AI behavior into predictable, safe, and governed workflows by running deterministic code at specific lifecycle checkpoints.

There’s no new resource type or integration to adopt. You automatically get both updates in the AgentCore harness you already use.

It has been revealed that strands harness provides an assembled agent foundation with recommended instructions, tools, and context management. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore harness operates that foundation as a managed AWS service. The result is a production-grade default agent that doesn’t require you to assemble and operate the harness or its infrastructure yourself.

According to recent reports, you do not need to provision compute, bundle and host the agent loop, manage session scaling, or operate tool-execution infrastructure. Each session runs in a secure, kernel-isolated microVM in AgentCore runtime, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, with managed compute, scaling, and high availability.

In a recent development, agentCore achieves this by connecting the harness to the services required for production agents, including session persistence, streaming responses, usage metadata, observability, AgentCore memory, Identity, Gateway, Browser, Code Interpreter, and customer-provided containers. You retain control over the model, instructions, tools, permissions, and lifecycle policies while AgentCore manages the underlying execution environment.

Harness now provides a stronger experience when you use its managed defaults:.

Customer-provided Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers, AgentCore Gateway (a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore), Browser, Code Interpreter, inline functions, skills, memory, and customer-provided containers continue to work through the existing harness interfaces.

Harness manages its defaults so that agents using them receive the current AgentCore recommended experience as models, instructions, context management, and built-in capabilities improve.

Explicit configuration always takes precedence:.

When allowedTools is omitted or set to ["*"], Harness provides the current recommended built-in tool set. Because this set can gain capabilities over time, applications with a fixed security or capability boundary should list only the tools they need.

For example, the following configuration permits read-only filesystem access and web retrieval without granting shell access or file modification:.

It has been revealed that with lifecycle hooks, you can run your own deterministic code at defined points in the agent loop. For example, an AWS Lambda function can allow or deny a request or a tool call, and an Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS) topic or Amazon EventBridge event bus can receive a notification to record activity or start an asynchronous workflow.

Harness supports four lifecycle events:.

Only Lambda hooks can change the agent loop. They run synchronously and return allow or deny, with an optional reason. SNS and Amazon EventBridge hooks are notifications and don’t block the agent loop.

According to recent reports, for example, a customer-support agent can investigate an order on its own while a before_tool_call hook checks each refund against an approval limit before the refund tool runs. The following configuration attaches that Lambda function to the harness:.

The function receives the proposed tool call in the hook payload and returns a decision:.

When the function denies the call, the harness skips the refund and the agent continues, so it can tell the customer that the request was escalated. Each decision also appears in the InvokeHarness response stream as a hookEvent:.

Hooks also apply to subagents. When the agent delegates a task, each tool call the subagent makes runs through the same beforeToolCall and afterToolCall hooks, so delegation can’t bypass your refund policy. The invocation-level hooks (beforeInvocation, afterInvocation) run once for the whole invocation.

You configure hooks with CreateHarness or UpdateHarness. If a Lambda function times out or returns an error, the hook applies its failureMode, which defaults to deny. For timeouts, payload fields, and context limits, see Lifecycle hooks in the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Developer Guide.

To see every event and target type working together, try the Refund Desk sample in the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore samples repository on GitHub. A six-step guided tour highlights all four lifecycle events and the AWS Lambda, Amazon SNS, and Amazon EventBridge targets. It also shows validation of client-supplied inline function results and the difference between failureMode deny and allow.

Industry observers note that creating a harness takes a single command. You name it and set up the instructions, context policy, and limits you want. This example creates a Research Coordinator: a harness with a task-oriented system prompt and summarization-based truncation. In a single invocation, it runs a researcher, a synthesizer, and a reviewer as subagents and returns one consolidated report. You get multi-agent orchestration and context management without provisioning infrastructure or wiring the delegation yourself.

The agentcore harness commands call the harness APIs directly, so you don’t need a CLI project or a deployment step. Install the AgentCore CLI, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, with npm:.

In a recent development, the CLI uses your default AWS credentials. It has no --profile flag, so set the AWS_PROFILE environment variable if you want a specific profile. Save the coordinator’s instructions from the sample as system_prompt.md in your working directory.

This command passes the coordinator’s system prompt, a summarization policy that keeps the 30 most recent messages intact as the conversation grows, and limits high enough for the full workflow. Because it omits the model, memory, and execution role, the harness uses the current AgentCore recommended model and managed memory, and the CLI creates an execution role in IAM for you.

In a recent development, creation is asynchronous. Wait for creation to finish. The last command should print READY:.

In a recent development, invoke your harness with a new session ID. Start with a basic question. The coordinator answers it directly, without calling its subagents:.

It has been revealed that then ask for a full research report in the same session. The coordinator intends the work and delegates to the researcher, synthesizer, and reviewer in order. It runs at most one revision cycle if the reviewer asks for it, and delivers the final report. Reusing the session ID continues the conversation in the same environment.

With --prompt, the CLI prints the completed transcript as JSON when the turn finishes. The research run takes about 10 to 15 minutes. To follow along as it works, leave out --prompt, and the CLI opens an interactive chat.

The same example in Python (boto3), including the full system prompt, is available in the AgentCore samples repository on GitHub.

Delete the harness when you’re done. This also deletes its managed memory unless you pass --delete-managed-memory false. The execution role that the CLI created stays in your account, so delete it in the IAM console if you no longer need it.

On November 11, AgentCore harness began rolling out the Strands harness-backed experience to new and existing harnesses. No customer action is required.

In a recent development, configuration you explicitly provide remains unchanged. Harnesses that omit the model, system prompt, or truncation configuration, or use allowedTools: ["*"], receive the upgraded managed defaults.

If your application requires fixed behavior or a fixed capability boundary, configure those settings explicitly.

Create and invoke an AgentCore harness as you do today. Use the managed defaults for the complete current recommended experience, or configure individual settings when your application requires fixed behavior.

We look forward to seeing what you build with the upgraded AgentCore harness.

Tech Report: Inside Amazon Connect Talent: The science of structured AI interviews

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1507 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Amazon

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • For organizations hiring hundreds or thousands of people, every interview presents the same challenge: How do you give candidates a consistent opportunity to demonstrate their skills while gathering the evidence needed to make informed hiring decisions?
  • Structured behavioral interviews offer a research-backed approach to this challenge.
  • Recent findings suggest that amazon Connect Talent brings established hiring science to AI-led interviews at scale.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

For organizations hiring hundreds or thousands of people, every interview presents the same challenge: How do you give candidates a consistent opportunity to demonstrate their skills while gathering the evidence needed to make informed hiring decisions?

Structured behavioral interviews offer a research-backed approach to this challenge. They use consistent, job-related questions and clear scoring criteria to give candidates an opportunity to demonstrate their skills. Decades of research in industrial-organizational (I-O) psychology have shown that structured interviews help organizations evaluate candidates and predict job performance (Schmidt & Hunter, 1998; Sackett et al., 2022). Yet delivering structured interviews at scale requires significant time and expertise to develop competencies, create questions, train interviewers, and evaluate responses consistently.

Recent findings suggest that amazon Connect Talent brings established hiring science to AI-led interviews at scale. Connect Talent uses structured questions, adaptive follow-ups, and evidence-based scoring to help organizations gather consistent, job-related information while giving more candidates the opportunity to demonstrate their strengths.

We built Connect Talent around three core design principles and evaluated how well the service applies them through a combination of internal research and independent expert review. The findings offer a closer look at the science behind Connect Talent’s AI-led, structured interviewing.

Connect Talent builds each interview around the competencies required for the role. The service uses job requirements and established occupational frameworks to create behaviorally anchored scorecards. Each scorecard defines specific strength and concern signals, and every interview question targets the behaviors it aims to uncover.

According to recent reports, the AI interviewer also adapts to each response. After every answer, it checks whether the candidate has provided enough evidence for the competency being assessed. When details are missing, it asks targeted follow-up questions. This approach preserves the structure of the interview while giving candidates more opportunities to explain their experience.

Connect Talent separates the interview conversation from the evaluation. The AI interviewer gathers evidence but does not assign scores. Afterward, a separate evaluation process identifies which behaviors the candidate demonstrated and cites the supporting transcript passages.

The service calculates each competency score from 1 to 5 using a fixed formula. When the transcript lacks sufficient evidence, Connect Talent flags the competency instead of producing a score. Hiring teams can review the evidence behind each rating, and missing evidence does not automatically count against the candidate.

Recent findings suggest that connect Talent evaluates transcribed candidate responses without using video, voice tone, or physical appearance to calculate competency scores. The service also excludes candidate identity information from scoring and evaluates each competency separately. These safeguards help focus assessments on job-related behaviors and limit the influence of unrelated information.

To understand how well these design principles work in practice, we combined independent I-O psychology evaluations with internal research. We examined whether the service generates job-relevant interview content, identifies behavioral evidence in line with expert assessments, gathers more complete responses through follow-up questions, and distinguishes between levels of demonstrated competency.

The quality of a structured interview starts with the skills it measures. Candidates need questions that reflect the requirements of the role, and hiring teams need confidence that the interview assesses those skills.

Amazon engaged an independent I-O psychology firm to evaluate Connect Talent’s AI-generated interview content. The firm reviewed the service’s baseline output before human editing and examined how well its competencies, questions, and rubrics aligned with job requirements. The evaluation found that Connect Talent retained critical job information in 100% of the job descriptions reviewed. Of the competencies generated, 91% were clearly traceable to the job description. The firm’s psychologists also found that 98% of interview questions targeted the intended competencies, and 94% of rubric signals clearly measured the intended competency.

These findings show that Connect Talent generated job-relevant interview content that met independent expert criteria in a vast majority of cases. Hiring teams can then review, select, and edit the competencies, scorecards, and questions before using them. This human oversight gives organizations control over the interview process while helping them apply structured hiring practices at scale.

Relevant questions provide the foundation for a structured interview. The next challenge is evaluating the evidence candidates provide with consistency.

To examine this, an independent I-O psychology firm reviewed 36 interviews assessing whether candidates demonstrated specific strengths and concerns, creating 252 rubric signals.

According to recent reports, connect Talent evaluated the same transcripts, reviewed hundreds of rubric signals, and aligned with expert scoring decisions in 89.3% of cases. Scoring alignment reached 97.6% when candidates provided clear evidence and 92.9% when only considering candidate concern signals, which identify behaviors that may indicate a poor fit for the intended role.

Sources indicate that the evaluation also produced a Cohen’s kappa of 0.79, a statistical measure that eliminates random chance coincidence. A Cohen’s kappa of 0.79 is just under the standard of 0.81 for almost perfect agreement. This outcome indicates substantial agreement between Connect Talent and the independent expert candidate scoring.

In a recent development, candidates may have relevant experience but leave important details out of their first response. In a traditional one-way video interview, a candidate may receive a fixed question and have only one opportunity to answer it. Hiring teams must then evaluate the information available, even when the response leaves many important questions unanswered.

Recent findings suggest that connect Talent uses adaptive follow-ups to gather more complete evidence. For example, a candidate might describe improving a slow system. The AI interviewer can ask what changed, which actions the candidate took, and how they measured the improvement. These questions help candidates explain their contributions and results in greater detail.

We studied the impact of follow-up questions by comparing assessments based on a candidate’s first response with assessments based on the full interview conversation. In a preliminary evaluation, scores based only on the first response were up to 1.14 points lower on a five-point scale than scores based on the full conversation. Assessments using the full conversation also came closer to expert evaluations.

Without follow-up questions, the scoring process identified fewer strength signals and more concern signals. In some cases, the candidate’s initial response simply lacked the information needed to demonstrate a relevant behavior. The full conversation captured more of what candidates demonstrated and gave hiring teams a more complete record of their experience.

Industry observers note that hiring teams need scores that reflect meaningful differences in demonstrated skills. Yet research has found that some AI scoring approaches concentrate ratings within a narrow range, making those differences harder to recognize (Zhu et al., 2026).

Connect Talent uses behaviorally anchored scorecards to evaluate specific strength and concern signals. Rather than asking an AI model to assign an overall rating, the service identifies evidence for each behavior and calculates the competency score using a predefined formula.

Consider the competency “collaboration”. A general AI scoring approach might evaluate a candidate’s overall collaboration skills based on the interview transcript. Connect Talent examines specific behaviors, such as whether the candidate sought input from colleagues before making a decision. Each finding contributes to the final score.

According to recent reports, we evaluated this approach across hundreds of expert-rated interview assessments. Connect Talent’s structured scoring used all five points of the rating scale, while holistic LLM-as-judge scoring concentrated its ratings within the middle three points.

In a recent development, this wider distribution allows the scoring system to represent more levels of demonstrated competency. The behaviorally anchored scorecards also help hiring teams understand the evidence behind each rating.

In a recent development, connect Talent brings the rigor of structured interviewing to more people while giving each candidate a meaningful chance to demonstrate their skills. The result is a new opportunity for organizations hiring at scale: more candidates can show what they can do, and more hiring teams can make decisions grounded in the evidence that matters.

Join us at AWS re:Invent 2026 for BIZ332: Every Candidate, Every Time: AI-Led Structured Interviews with Amazon Connect Talent, an interactive Chalk Talk led by Sunitha Srivatsa and Gerald Friedland.

The session will explore the science behind Connect Talent, including structured interviewing, adaptive follow-up questions, and evidence-based scoring.

Industry News: Transformers Model Integration Contracts

📅 03 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1313 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • On July 30, 2026, Transformers enabled PyTorch's scaled dot-product attention (SDPA) for T5.
  • Recent findings suggest that when we later replayed those commits, a small UMT5 model running on CPU flagged it on every one of them.
  • Industry observers note that transformers supports over 750 model types, and its test suite is big: 88,000+ CPU tests on main, plus 200,000+ GPU tests in a daily run.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

On July 30, 2026, Transformers enabled PyTorch's scaled dot-product attention (SDPA) for T5. As a side effect, UMT5's decoder could attend to future tokens. During training, it could peek at the answer it was supposed to predict. Nothing crashed, and the bug stayed in main for almost two months.

Recent findings suggest that when we later replayed those commits, a small UMT5 model running on CPU flagged it on every one of them. This post is about that model and the tests built around it.

Industry observers note that transformers supports over 750 model types, and its test suite is big: 88,000+ CPU tests on main, plus 200,000+ GPU tests in a daily run. Model tests are only part of it: we also test pipelines, training, distributed execution, quantization and attention kernels.

In a recent development, the integration tests load real checkpoints and exercise the model's API on real hardware. Running all of that on every PR would mean keeping a lot of GPUs busy all day long, which isn't practical. By the time a scheduled run finds a regression, it may already be in main.

Sources indicate that our approach is to shrink the model instead. We build a fixture: a small model made from the real checkpoint's configuration, with fewer and narrower layers but every kind of layer it has, and its tokenizer and processor files unchanged. It is published once, then reused. We run "fast integration tests" against it on a cheap CPU runner. In our CPU study, the experimental UMT5 fixture used 66 MB of weights; the source checkpoint is 1,227 MB.

This also covers very large models: some don't fit on our standard GPU runners, but their fixtures run on CPU.

Model integrators already build tiny test models (Transformers' tiny-random-* checkpoints). We wanted a common recipe, and checks that go beyond loading the model and running a forward pass. The UMT5 bug would have passed a forward pass just fine.

Fixtures won't replace full integration tests, but on PRs they give us a chance to catch bugs before they reach main.

According to recent reports, transformers-mic is a proposed standard for packaging these tests. A Model Integration Contract (MIC) has three parts:.

The contract holds if running the usage path on the fixture still produces the baselines.

A contract covers an architecture and a usage path, not a single checkpoint: compatible checkpoints can share a fixture, while each keeps its own expected results. We publish them in huggingface-mic.

According to recent reports, for example, the SmolLM contract generates from prompts such as "The capital of France is" and compares its token IDs with a recorded answer. After loading the model and tokenizer, the generation code is, simplified to one prompt:.

According to recent reports, it also compares training loss, checks that gradients are finite and verifies that an optimizer step changes the weights. See the full usage.md.

In a recent development, A fleet dataset on the Hub pins each MIC to a frozen revision, along with the package versions used to record its baselines. Each CI run records the fleet revision it used, so we can reproduce it later.

On a PR, we pick MICs based on the files the patch changes.

Industry observers note that we replayed frozen MICs over five months of Transformers commits. The small UMT5 fixture flagged the regression from its introduction on July 30, 2026 until its fix on September 28. Label log-probabilities differed from the reviewed baseline by 1.22 and training loss by about 0.20.

One detail mattered: the contract used SDPA, the default attention path. Running only the eager attention variant missed the bug. A fixture only helps if it goes through the same code as the real checkpoint.

We then reverted the fix on a proof branch in Transformers' CI. The check failed with the same differences, and the selected T5 contract's runner step took 13.4 seconds on CPU, excluding setup.

The replay results and the CI demo have the measurements and reproduction details.

Sources indicate that the first recipe was simple: make the dimensions smaller and keep fewer layers. That wasn't enough for mixed architectures. Keeping two layers is no use if both use sliding attention and the full-attention layers disappear.

We also keep the original weights file format. Otherwise we would skip the conversion code that runs when a user loads the real checkpoint. The full recipe has more detail.

Sources indicate that the Llama 4 Scout shrink report highlights what this looks like on a significant model. 108.6 billion parameters become 44.7 million. The vision stack goes from 34 layers to 2 and the language stack from 48 to 4, keeping the checked layer kinds and MoE routing style.

According to recent reports, our CLI, tmic, creates the contract and builds the fixture. For a latest model, an LLM drafts the usage code and manifest, and CPU and GPU runs measure the candidate baselines. The LLM drafts; it doesn't approve. Changed expectations require human review.

To try it on your machine, use your source checkpoint in place of org/model:.

Recent findings suggest that it drafts the contract, builds the fixture and records its baselines on your machine, asking you to review each step, and stops before uploading anything. For a newly introduced model, the draft comes from an LLM through Inference Providers, billed to your own account (--bill-to ''). The CLI docs cover the individual steps.

Recent findings suggest that we used agents to build MICs across model families. When they hit an edge case, we fixed the recipe itself rather than the one fixture, with help from model experts. The published models and remaining gaps are in the coverage space.

Sources indicate that with random weights, our Whisper fixture barely responded to changes in the audio. It ran, but that made it a poor test of the audio path.

Industry observers note that so we trained it on a few tones paired with words such as "red" and "green". We weren't teaching it speech recognition, just making audio changes visible in its outputs. In our weight-initialization study, the random Whisper fixtures caught 18 of 24 injected faults. The overfit fixtures caught all 24.

That gives us two ways to build the weights:.

The Whisper result doesn't settle which is better. Those were synthetic faults, and we haven't found a real regression caught only by the overfit version. Both versions missed an assisted-decoding bug that the real Whisper checkpoint exposed.

Recent findings suggest that so we keep random weights when they pass the checks, and overfit when we need better sensitivity or readable answers. Training takes seconds, but it is one more step that can fail to converge, and one more thing to maintain. The comparison has the results for both.

It has been revealed that as of November 1, 2026, the MIC job in Transformers CI reports failures without blocking PRs. Whether it should block depends on things we haven't measured yet:.

We also don't know how many bugs, like the Whisper assisted-decoding one, only show up with real weights, or whether overfitting catches real bugs that random weights miss.

Coverage is still partial, across model families and the APIs people use. When a regression slips through, we can add the missing usage path and replay it on the broken and fixed versions. We'll keep existing tests until their coverage is accounted for.

Finally, we'd like to link original Hub model pages to their MICs, so a developer or an agent using a checkpoint could start from an example tested on that checkpoint, its environment and its expected outputs.

In a recent development, want to help? Pick an uncovered model from the coverage space, try the tmic workflow, and contribute a usage path or review a generated contract.
